noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: know that the mole (mol) is the unit for the amount of a substance and be able to perform calculations using the Avogadro constant L (6.02 x 1023 mol-1)

primer.text: Chemists cannot tally atoms one by one, so the mole bundles particles into a countable package of exactly 6.02 x 10^23. This note fixes the Avogadro constant, defines the mole against the carbon-12 benchmark, and builds the two conversions - mass to moles, moles to particles - that every later calculation reuses.

lessons.title: What the mole counts
lessons.opening: Chemists cannot tally atoms one by one, so the mole bundles particles into a countable package of exactly 6.02 x 10^23. This lesson defines the Avogadro constant, shows why the same number works for atoms, molecules, ions and electrons, and fixes what one mole of any substance weighs.
keyPoints: The Avogadro constant L is 6.02 x 10^23 mol^-1, the number of particles in one mole.
The constant applies equally to atoms, molecules, ions and electrons.
A mole is the amount of substance that contains this number of fundamental units.
One mole of an element weighs, in grams, the value of its relative atomic mass.
The molar mass links a mole of particles to the 12.00 g of carbon-12 benchmark.

low.restatement: A mole is just a gigantic counting unit: pick 6.02 x 10^23 of anything chemical and you are holding one mole of it.
low.analogy: The mole plays the part of a dozen in baking - a fixed tally that converts between what you count and what you can weigh out on a balance.
low.examPointer: Learn the constant's value and unit exactly: 6.02 x 10^23 mol^-1 earns the mark; 6.02 x 10^23 alone does not.

medium.restatement: The Avogadro constant is the bridge between a countable amount and a mass: one mole of particles has a mass in grams numerically equal to the relative mass of one particle.
medium.analogy: Imagine scaling a single sweet up to a sack: the relative atomic mass is the label on one sweet, and a mole is the sack whose weight in grams matches that label.
medium.examPointer: When a question says 'exactly 12.00 g of carbon-12', it is anchoring the mole definition - quote that anchor when asked to define amount of substance.

check.stem: What does the Avogadro constant measure?

options.text: The number of particles in one mole of a substance
options.explanation: The constant is defined as the particle count per mole, 6.02 x 10^23 mol^-1.

options.text: The mass of one mole of a substance in grams
options.explanation: Mass per mole is the molar mass, not the Avogadro constant.

options.text: The volume occupied by one mole of any gas
options.explanation: Volume per mole of gas is the molar gas volume, covered elsewhere.

options.text: The charge carried by one mole of electrons
options.explanation: Charge per mole of electrons is the Faraday constant, a different quantity.

check.stem: Which particles can be counted in moles?

options.text: Atoms, molecules, ions and electrons alike
options.explanation: The constant is particle-agnostic: any fundamental chemical particle can be tallied in moles.

options.text: Atoms only, because the mole is defined from carbon-12
options.explanation: The carbon-12 anchor fixes the scale but does not restrict what is counted.

options.text: Molecules only, since moles describe compounds
options.explanation: Elements are counted in moles just as readily as compounds.

options.text: Ions only, because moles require a charge
options.explanation: Moles count amount of substance; charge is irrelevant to the tally.

check.stem: One mole of carbon atoms has a mass of 12.00 g. What mass does one mole of magnesium atoms have? (Ar of Mg = 24.3)
check.misconceptionClass: mole mass equals Ar in grams

options.explanation: One mole of an element weighs its relative atomic mass in grams.
That is the carbon benchmark, not magnesium's.
The Avogadro constant is a particle count, not a mass.
That would be two moles of magnesium.

check.stem: A sample contains 3.01 x 10^23 molecules of a gas. Roughly how many moles is that?

options.explanation: Dividing by 6.02 x 10^23 gives about half a mole.
One mole is 6.02 x 10^23 particles, twice the sample.
That would need about 1.2 x 10^24 particles.
Moles are of order unity here; the raw count is not the mole number.

check.stem: Why do reaction calculations lean on the mole and the Avogadro constant?

options.text: It converts between a countable number of particles and a weighable mass
options.explanation: The constant links the microscopic count to grams on a balance.

options.text: It fixes the temperature at which reactions occur
options.explanation: The mole says nothing about temperature.

options.text: It measures how fast a reaction proceeds
options.explanation: Rate is a separate kinetic quantity.

options.text: It determines whether a reaction is exothermic
options.explanation: Energetics are unrelated to the particle tally.

check.stem: State the value and unit of the Avogadro constant.
check.modelAnswer: The Avogadro constant L is 6.02 x 10^23 mol^-1, the number of particles in one mole of a substance.

check.stem: Define the mole in terms of the Avogadro constant.
check.modelAnswer: A mole is the amount of substance that contains 6.02 x 10^23 fundamental units, the same number of particles as there are atoms in exactly 12.00 g of carbon-12.

check.stem: A student says one mole of oxygen molecules and one mole of oxygen atoms describe the same amount of matter. Explain why the statement is wrong.
check.modelAnswer: One mole always contains the same number of particles, but an oxygen molecule holds two atoms, so a mole of molecules contains twice as many oxygen atoms as a mole of atoms; the amounts of matter differ by a factor of two.

check.stem: A jeweller weighs out 4.82 g of silver (Ar = 107.9). Calculate the number of silver atoms supplied, giving your answer to 3 s.f.

lessons.title: Working the mole ladder
lessons.opening: Every stoichiometry chain runs through the same ladder: mass to moles with n = m/M, then moles to particles with the Avogadro constant. This lesson drills that ladder in both directions, including the very large and very small answers the constant naturally produces.
keyPoints: The linking equation is n = m / M for mass in grams and molar mass in g mol^-1.
Particles divide by the Avogadro constant to give moles, and moles multiply by it to give particles.
Answers after using the constant are often very large or very small by nature.
One mole of water weighs 18.0 g because two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom make up each molecule.

low.restatement: To get moles, divide mass by molar mass or divide particles by the big constant; to leave moles, do the opposite.
low.analogy: Think of two doors into the same room: the mass door and the particle door both lead to the mole counter in the middle.
low.examPointer: Show the ladder in your working - method marks survive even when an arithmetic slip lands.

medium.restatement: The molar mass converts grams to moles, and the Avogadro constant converts moles to a particle census; chaining both maps a weighable sample onto the atoms inside it.
medium.analogy: Currency exchange works the same way: pounds to a currency-neutral amount, then to another currency - here grams to moles, then to particles.
medium.examPointer: Do not round the mole value before multiplying by the constant; carry at least 3 s.f. through the chain.

check.stem: What is the molar mass of water, H2O?

options.explanation: Two hydrogens at 1.0 plus one oxygen at 16.0 give 18.0 g mol^-1.
That is the oxygen alone; the two hydrogens add 2.0.
Adding only one hydrogen misses the second.
No atomic mass combination of H2O reaches 20.0.

check.stem: How many moles are present in 100 g of water? (Mr = 18.0)

options.explanation: That inverts the division; 1800 g would be 100 mol.
That is half the correct quotient.
Mass in grams is not itself a mole count.

check.stem: Which expression gives the number of molecules in n moles of a gas?

options.explanation: Moles multiply by the Avogadro constant to give a particle count.
Division shrinks the count; particles exceed moles.
24.0 dm^3 is the molar gas volume, not a particle count.
18.0 is water's molar mass, irrelevant to a particle census.

check.stem: Five hundred million platinum atoms were counted out. Without calculating, what kind of mass should be expected? (Ar of Pt = 195.1)

options.text: A vanishingly small mass, far below a microgram
options.explanation: So few particles is about 8.3 x 10^-16 mol, giving about 1.6 x 10^-13 g.

options.text: About one gram, comparable to a coin
options.explanation: A gram of platinum holds vastly more than 5 x 10^8 atoms.
A kilogram of platinum contains near 3 x 10^24 atoms.
That mass corresponds to one full mole, not a fraction.

check.stem: A chemist has 0.0218 mol of ethanol and needs its mass. Using the linking equation and molar mass, what value results? (Mr of C2H5OH = 46.0)

options.explanation: 0.0218 mol on 46.0 g mol^-1 lands at 1.00 g - a huge molecular count inside one gram.
That would be one mole, roughly 46 times more.
That reads the mole value as grams.
The multiplication is halved; 0.0218 mol on 46.0 lands at 1.00.

check.stem: State the equation linking moles n, mass m and molar mass M.
check.modelAnswer: The linking equation is n = m / M, with mass in grams and molar mass in g mol^-1.

check.stem: State the two-step chain that converts the mass of a compound into the number of its molecules.
check.modelAnswer: First divide the mass by the molar mass to obtain moles, then multiply the moles by the Avogadro constant to obtain the number of molecules.

check.stem: Explain why answers that follow from dividing by the Avogadro constant can be far smaller than 1 without being wrong.
check.modelAnswer: The constant is an enormous tally, about 6.02 x 10^23 particles per mole, so a sample containing only a few hundred million particles corresponds to a fraction of a mole around 10^-16 mol, and its mass shrinks accordingly.

check.stem: Calculate the number of water molecules in 100 g of water, running n = 100 / 18.0 then the Avogadro constant. Give the answer to 3 s.f.
check.modelAnswer: n = 100 / 18.0 = 5.56 mol; molecules = 5.56 x 6.02 x 10^23 gives 3.35 x 10^24 molecules.

glossary.definition: The amount of substance containing 6.02 x 10^23 fundamental units, the same particle count as exactly 12.00 g of carbon-12.
The mass of one mole of a substance, quoted in g mol^-1.
The particle count per mole, 6.02 x 10^23 mol^-1, applied to atoms, molecules, ions and electrons.

workedExample.prompt: How many moles and how many molecules are present in 100 g of water? (Mr = 18.0)
steps: Convert mass to moles: n = m / M = 100 / 18.0 = 5.56 mol (3 s.f.).
Convert moles to molecules: 5.56 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 3.35 x 10^24 molecules.
workedExample.finalAnswer: 5.56 mol, which is 3.35 x 10^24 molecules of water.
